title: datetime: Work With Dates Without Getting the Math Wrong
excerpt: Create dates, add days, measure gaps with timedelta, and format or parse text dates using Python's datetime module.

headings.text: Add and Subtract Time With timedelta

html:
How many days are there between 10 February and 5 March? You cannot just subtract the numbers: months have different lengths, leap years add a day, and weeks wrap around. Date arithmetic is full of small traps, and code that handles them by hand is almost always wrong somewhere.

Python's datetime module gives you real date and time objects that already know the calendar, so you can add, subtract, compare and format dates safely. This lesson covers the four things you will use most: creating dates, doing arithmetic with them, formatting them as text, and reading text back into dates.

Create a Date

The module datetime contains tools for dates, and the line from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta brings in three of them by name (one is also called datetime, like the module). The date tool takes a year, a month and a day. The examples use fixed dates so the output is always the same:

from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta

d = date(2026, 3, 5)

print(d)
print(d.year, d.month, d.day)
print(d.weekday())
print(d.strftime("%A"))
2026-03-05
2026 3 5
3
Thursday

The method weekday() returns a number where Monday is 0, so 3 means Thursday, which the last line confirms by asking for the full day name. To get today's date, write date.today(); its result of course depends on when you run it.

Subtract Two Dates

Subtracting one date from another gives a timedelta, an object that represents a length of time. Why not just subtract the day numbers yourself? Because that breaks across month ends, and Python does the calendar work for you:

gap = date(2026, 3, 5) - date(2026, 2, 10)

print(gap)
print(gap.days)
23 days, 0:00:00
23

That answers the opening question without any month-length arithmetic: Python knew how many days February has. (A timedelta also stores hours, minutes and seconds; the 0:00:00 part is zero here.)

Add and Subtract Time With timedelta

You can also build a timedelta yourself and add it to a date to move forward or backward:

print(d + timedelta(days=30))
print(d - timedelta(weeks=2))
2026-04-04
2026-02-19

A date has no time of day. When you need hours and minutes, use datetime, which works the same way:

meeting = datetime(2026, 3, 5, 14, 30)
later = meeting + timedelta(hours=10)

print(meeting)
print(later)
print((later - meeting).total_seconds())
2026-03-05 14:30:00
2026-03-06 00:30:00
36000.0

Adding ten hours to 14:30 rolled over into the next day automatically. And total_seconds() turns any timedelta into a plain number of seconds, which is handy for comparisons.

Format a Date as Text

The method strftime() (think "string from time") turns a date into text using codes that start with a percent sign:

print(meeting.strftime("%d %B %Y, %H:%M"))
print(meeting.strftime("%d/%m/%y"))
print(meeting.strftime("%A"))
05 March 2026, 14:30
05/03/26
Thursday

What do the codes mean? %d is the day, %m the month as a number, %B the full month name, %Y a four-digit year, %y a two-digit year, %H the hour (24-hour clock), %M the minute and %A the weekday name. Everything else you type, like the commas and slashes, is copied as it is.

Read a Date From Text

The reverse job is strptime() ("string parsed into time"): you give it the text and the format that describes it, and it builds a datetime:

christmas = datetime.strptime("25/12/2026", "%d/%m/%Y")

print(christmas)
print(christmas.strftime("%A"))
2026-12-25 00:00:00
Friday

The format must describe the text exactly. If it does not, Python refuses rather than guess, with a ValueError, which means the value is the right kind of thing but not acceptable here:

datetime.strptime("2026-12-25", "%d/%m/%Y")
ValueError: time data '2026-12-25' does not match format '%d/%m/%Y'

Compare Dates

Dates compare with the usual operators. Can they be sorted like numbers? Yes, so you can test whether something is late or sort a list of events (inside a list, each date is shown in its longer developer form):

deadline = date(2026, 3, 31)

print(d < deadline)
print(sorted([date(2026, 5, 1), date(2026, 1, 15), date(2026, 3, 5)]))
True
[datetime.date(2026, 1, 15), datetime.date(2026, 3, 5), datetime.date(2026, 5, 1)]

A Note on Time Zones

The objects in this lesson are "naive": they carry no time zone, so 14:30 means 14:30 in whatever place the program is thinking about. That is fine for simple scheduling, deadlines and age calculations. When your program must compare moments across regions, use time-zone-aware datetimes instead, which Python supports through its zoneinfo module.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonDatetime.ipynb.

Summary

  • date(year, month, day) and datetime(year, month, day, hour, minute) create calendar-aware objects.
  • Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta; .days and .total_seconds() read it as numbers.
  • Add or subtract timedelta(days=..., hours=...) to move a date forward or backward.
  • strftime(format) turns a date into text; strptime(text, format) reads text into a datetime.
  • The format must match the text exactly, otherwise a ValueError is raised.
  • Dates can be compared with < and > and sorted like numbers.
